Course-design sources

Why this design? Sources and examples

The lemonade story is a fictional illustration. These sources inform the teaching moves; they do not test this module or guarantee outcomes.

  • Align the activity and assessment with what students should learn. Carnegie Mellon Eberly Center

    How we apply it: Ask for a learning goal and preserve requirements when revising directions.

    Carnegie Mellon University, Eberly Center. Why should assessments, learning objectives, and instructional strategies be aligned? (n.d.).

  • Scenario-based discussion strategies produced different patterns of exploration, integration, and resolution. Darabi et al. (2011)

    How we apply it: Give peers a specific decision to examine in the fictional lemonade example.

    Darabi, A., Arrastia, M. C., Nelson, D. W., Cornille, T., & Liang, X. (2011). Cognitive presence in asynchronous online learning: A comparison of four discussion strategies. Journal of Computer Assisted Learning, 27(3), 216–227.

  • Their feedback-literacy framework includes making judgments and taking action on feedback. Carless & Boud (2018)

    How we apply it: Ask students to explain how peer input informed a revision or defense.

    Carless, D., & Boud, D. (2018). The development of student feedback literacy: Enabling uptake of feedback. Assessment & Evaluation in Higher Education, 43(8), 1315–1325.
